idiom_name: module functions over stdlib sqlite3 (DB-API) with sqlite3.Row records
implementation_notes: The standard library's sqlite3 - and DB-API drivers such as psycopg for client-server databases - make the gateway a module of functions per table: one statement per function, executed with ? / %s placeholders, returning rows as tuples or, after con.row_factory = sqlite3.Row, as name-addressable records. This is the zero-dependency default and the closest to the catalog form: the SQL for a table lives in one module, and callers pass their connection so transactions stay outside.
pitfalls: sqlite3 connections are thread-bound (check_same_thread) and uncommitted work is rolled back when the connection closes - a gateway must not hide commit().
sqlite3.Row is not a dict: .get() does not exist and missing columns raise IndexError, so mapping helpers must use keys() or explicit defaults.
Sharing one Connection across threads without check_same_thread=False plus serialization corrupts writes; use a queue or a connection per thread.

variants.name: SQLAlchemy Core Table objects
variants.idiom_name: Table('users', metadata, ...) + select()/insert() executed on a Connection
variants.implementation_notes: SQLAlchemy Core turns the schema into Python objects: Table('users', metadata, Column(...)) is the per-table definition, select(users).where(users.c.id == id) and insert(users).values(...) are the statements, and conn.execute(...) returns Row/RowMapping records. It adds a schema layer and dialect portability (one gateway, several backends, parameterized by construction) while keeping statement-level control; choose it when the application already uses SQLAlchemy or must target more than one database, and keep raw driver calls where the schema layer adds nothing.
pitfalls: Table objects are tied to one MetaData and engine; reusing them across two engines or metadata registries breaks statement compilation in confusing ways.
A Session (ORM) flushes and commits implicitly while a Core Connection needs an explicit commit - mixing both on the same gateway loses writes.
Row is a tuple-like object, not a dict; code that expects mapping access must use ._mapping or .mappings().
